title: Financing: the one-year line, not long-looking terms (a: no)

state.clause: Payment. The license fee is payable in 12 equal monthly installments of $100,000, the first due on the delivery date.
state.context: Customer based in Germany. Perpetual software license for $1,200,000, delivered and transferred at signing. The vendor's standard payment terms are net 30.

financing_component_concept.instructions: Read with the deal information: under ASC 606, does `clause` raise the question of a significant financing component?

financing_component.instructions: Under `clause`, does more than one year separate when the customer receives the goods or services and when it pays, in either direction?

rationale: The last installment arrives 11 months after the license transfers, within one year, so the practical expedient applies (606-10-32-18) and no financing adjustment is needed, however long the terms look against net 30.
teaches: The same installment clause with 12 vs 16 monthly payments: 11 vs 15 months from transfer to the last one. Only that gap decides the label, not the wording or the departure from net 30.
weakness: Term of art read in its everyday sense: 'significant financing component' fires on long-looking terms that stay within a year.
heldout_evidence: rr-f3-h02 rule 0.24–0.25 in prose and structured, gold yes

title: Self-description: a clause that calls itself independent (a: yes)

state.clause: Supplemental Order. This Supplemental Order is a new and independent agreement and does not modify the Prior Order. Starting 1 August 2028, Customer purchases 400B tokens for use over twelve (12) months at $1.90 per 1M tokens ($760,000).
state.context: Prior Order: three-year term from 1 February 2026 to 31 January 2029 for 1,500B tokens and $3,000,000. SSP for committed tokens: $1.80 to $2.00 per 1M tokens. The Prior Order has no option to buy additional tokens.

contract_modification_concept.instructions: Read with the deal information: under ASC 606, is `clause` a contract modification?

contract_modification.instructions: Does `clause` change the scope or price of an existing contract with this customer? Exercising an option the existing contract already grants, on its stated terms, is not a change; neither is a new contract that starts when the old one expires.

rationale: It adds tokens while the Prior Order still runs, so it changes the scope of an existing arrangement: a contract modification (606-10-25-10), whatever the clause calls itself. At SSP with distinct goods it is accounted for as a separate contract (606-10-25-12), but it is still a modification, as in author-approved rr-f4-03.
teaches: Identical self-description in both. Only the start date decides: during the Prior Order (a modification) or at its expiry (a new contract).
weakness: The clause's own description believed: 'a new and independent agreement' read as not a modification.

title: Self-description: a clause that calls itself independent (b: no)

state.clause: Supplemental Order. This Supplemental Order is a new and independent agreement and does not modify the Prior Order. Starting 1 February 2029, Customer purchases 400B tokens for use over twelve (12) months at $1.90 per 1M tokens ($760,000).
state.context: Prior Order: three-year term from 1 February 2026 to 31 January 2029 for 1,500B tokens and $3,000,000. SSP for committed tokens: $1.80 to $2.00 per 1M tokens. The Prior Order has no option to buy additional tokens.

contract_modification.instructions: Does `clause` change the scope or price of an existing contract with this customer? Exercising an option the existing contract already grants, on its stated terms, is not a change; neither is a new contract that starts when the old one expires.

rationale: It starts when the Prior Order expires, so it is a new contract, not a change to the old one. The clause's description happens to be accurate.
teaches: Identical self-description in both. Only the start date decides: during the Prior Order (a modification) or at its expiry (a new contract).
weakness: The clause's own description believed: 'a new and independent agreement' read as not a modification.

title: Discount language: a 'preferred rate' inside vs below SSP (a: no)

state.clause: Preferred Pricing. In recognition of Customer's commitment, Customer may purchase additional tokens during the Term at a preferred rate of $1.85 per 1M tokens.
state.context: Customer: mid-market software company on a two-year term with a prepaid commitment of 800B tokens. SSP for committed tokens for customers of this size: $1.80 to $2.00 per 1M tokens.

material_right_concept.instructions: Read with the deal information: under ASC 606, does `clause` give the customer a material right?

material_right.instructions: Does `clause` give the customer an option to buy additional goods or services at a price below the low end of the standalone selling price range stated in the deal information? A purchase the customer has already committed to is not an option.

rationale: $1.85 is within the SSP range. Despite the word "preferred", the option gives no discount beyond what this class of customer would pay, so there is no material right (606-10-55-43).
teaches: The same 'preferred rate' clause at two prices. Only where the price sits against the SSP range decides.
weakness: Discount language triggers 'material right' without checking the price against the SSP range.
heldout_evidence: rr-f1-h04 rule 0.66–0.83 in structured and computed, gold no

title: Purchase vs option at the same discount (a: no)

state.clause: Year-Three Tokens. Customer purchases 300B additional tokens for use in the third contract year at $1.50 per 1M tokens.
state.context: New three-year order signed today. Customer: enterprise software company. Base commitment: 2,000B tokens at $1.90 per 1M tokens. SSP for committed tokens: $1.80 to $2.00 per 1M tokens.

material_right_concept.instructions: Read with the deal information: under ASC 606, does `clause` give the customer a material right?

material_right.instructions: Does `clause` give the customer an option to buy additional goods or services at a price below the low end of the standalone selling price range stated in the deal information? A purchase the customer has already committed to is not an option.

facts.price_vs_ssp: 17% below the low end of the SSP range

rationale: A committed purchase in the same contract, not an option. The $1.50 price is 17% below the low end of the SSP range, which affects how the transaction price is allocated (606-10-32-28 to 32-31), but there is no material right.
teaches: Same tokens, same price, same timing. Only 'purchases' vs 'may purchase up to' decides.
weakness: A committed purchase below SSP read as a material right, which needs an option.

title: Fixed vs variable: an unconditional vs a usage-conditioned credit (a: no)

state.clause: Annual Credit. For each of the first two contract years, Vendor will credit 10% of that year's fee ($96,000) against the next year's invoice.
state.context: Customer: enterprise software company on a three-year subscription at $960,000 per year, billed annually in advance. The vendor's standard order form has no credits.

variable_consideration_concept.instructions: Read with the deal information: under ASC 606, does `clause` involve variable consideration?

variable_consideration.instructions: Can the amount the customer pays under `clause` change depending on a future event, such as usage, performance, or service levels? A fixed amount, or a fixed unit price on purchases the customer chooses to make, is not variable.

rationale: Both credits are certain and fixed at signing, and each lands on an invoice inside the term. They lower the transaction price by $192,000, but nothing about them depends on a future event, so they are not variable consideration.
teaches: The same 10% credit. Only whether it depends on future usage decides.
weakness: A fixed price change read as variable consideration.

title: Fixed vs variable: an unconditional vs a usage-conditioned credit (b: yes)

state.clause: Annual Credit. For each of the first two contract years, if Customer's token usage in that year exceeds 600B tokens, Vendor will credit 10% of that year's fee ($96,000) against the next year's invoice.
state.context: Customer: enterprise software company on a three-year subscription at $960,000 per year, billed annually in advance. The vendor's standard order form has no credits.

variable_consideration_concept.instructions: Read with the deal information: under ASC 606, does `clause` involve variable consideration?

variable_consideration.instructions: Can the amount the customer pays under `clause` change depending on a future event, such as usage, performance, or service levels? A fixed amount, or a fixed unit price on purchases the customer chooses to make, is not variable.

rationale: The credit depends on future usage, so the amount the customer pays is uncertain at signing: variable consideration to estimate and possibly constrain (606-10-32-5 to 32-9).
teaches: The same 10% credit. Only whether it depends on future usage decides.

contract_modification_concept.instructions: Read with the deal information: under ASC 606, is `clause` a contract modification?
